section.title: Warning Against False Teachers
section.sectionRationale: The letter opens with its reason for being. Paul greets Timothy, then states the charge he left him at Ephesus: stop certain men from teaching a different doctrine. The false teaching is contrasted with the true goal of instruction, love from a pure heart, and with the proper, lawful use of the law, which agrees with the glorious gospel.
section.thesis: The church must guard sound doctrine, because false teaching breeds speculation and empty talk, while the aim of true instruction is love from a pure heart, a clear conscience, and a sincere faith, all in step with the glorious gospel of the blessed God.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the apostolic greeting to Timothy; the charge to silence those teaching a different doctrine; and the lawful use of the law over against those who misuse it.

units.label: Greeting to Timothy
units.note: apostle by the command of God

verses.text: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the command of God our Savior and of Christ Jesus our hope,
To Timothy, my true child in the faith: Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.

units.label: The charge against false teachers
units.note: the goal of instruction is love

verses.text: As I urged you on my departure to Macedonia, you should stay on at Ephesus to instruct certain men not to {{heterodidaskaleo|teach false doctrines}}
or devote themselves to {{mythos|myths}} and endless genealogies, which promote speculation rather than the {{oikonomia|stewardship}} of God’s work, which is by faith.
The goal of our instruction is the {{agape|love}} that comes from a pure heart, a clear {{syneidesis|conscience}}, and a sincere faith.
Some have strayed from these ways and turned aside to empty talk.
They want to be teachers of the law, but they do not understand what they are saying or that which they so confidently assert.

units.label: The lawful use of the law
units.note: in step with the glorious gospel

verses.text: Now we know that the {{nomos|law}} is good, if one uses it legitimately.
We realize that law is not enacted for the righteous, but for the lawless and rebellious, for the ungodly and sinful, for the unholy and profane, for killers of father or mother, for murderers,
for the sexually immoral, for homosexuals, for slave traders and liars and perjurers, and for anyone else who is averse to {{hygiaino|sound}} teaching
that agrees with the glorious {{euangelion|gospel}} of the blessed God, with which I have been entrusted.

heterodidaskaleo.gloss: To teach a different or other doctrine, from heteros, other, and didaskalos, teacher. It names teaching that departs from the apostolic gospel. The very charge of the letter is to stop such teaching at Ephesus; sound doctrine and different doctrine are the two poles the whole book moves between.

mythos.gloss: A myth, fable, or made-up tale, opposed to truth. Paul repeatedly warns Timothy against myths, here paired with endless genealogies. Such speculation feeds curiosity and pride but not faith, standing in contrast to the stewardship of God's work.

oikonomia.gloss: Household management, stewardship, or God's ordered plan. The gospel advances God's stewardship, His saving administration, received by faith, not the endless speculation the false teachers prize. Sound teaching serves God's work; myths only distract from it.

agape.gloss: Self-giving love, the highest New Testament word for love. Paul names it as the goal of all true instruction: not mere knowledge or debate, but love flowing from a pure heart, a clear conscience, and sincere faith. Doctrine that does not lead to love has missed its aim.

syneidesis.gloss: Conscience, the inner witness that judges right and wrong. A clear conscience is one of the three springs of genuine love. The false teachers, by contrast, have shipwrecked faith and conscience together; a defiled conscience and false doctrine travel as companions.

nomos.gloss: The law, especially the law of Moses. Paul affirms the law is good when used lawfully: it exposes sin and restrains the lawless, driving sinners to the gospel. The would-be teachers of the law misuse it, not grasping what they so confidently assert.

hygiaino.gloss: To be healthy or sound, the root of our word hygiene. A signature word of the Pastoral Epistles for doctrine that is spiritually wholesome and health-giving. Sound teaching agrees with the gospel; whatever is contrary to it is, by implication, diseased.

euangelion.gloss: Gospel, good news. Paul calls it the glorious gospel of the blessed God, entrusted to him as a stewardship. It is the measuring line for all teaching: sound doctrine agrees with the gospel, and the law itself, rightly used, points toward it.

basic.context: Paul greets Timothy as his true child in the faith and reminds him why he was left at Ephesus: to stop certain men from teaching a different doctrine full of myths and endless genealogies. That teaching produces speculation and empty talk; the true aim of instruction is love from a pure heart. Paul then shows that the law is good when used lawfully, to expose sin, and that it agrees with the gospel entrusted to him.
basic.hermeneutics: Paul is charging a younger pastor to protect a church from error. The passage is prescriptive about guarding sound doctrine and about the goal of teaching being love, not just knowledge. The list of sins in verses 9 and 10 shows the law's proper use, exposing sin, not a checklist to condemn without hope, since the gospel that follows is for exactly such sinners.
basic.originalLanguages: The false teachers heterodidaskaleo, teach a different doctrine, chasing mythos, myths, instead of God's oikonomia, stewardship. The goal of true instruction is agape, love, from a pure heart and a clear syneidesis, conscience. The nomos, law, is good when used lawfully, and sound, hygiaino, teaching agrees with the euangelion, the glorious gospel of the blessed God.
basic.typology: The law that exposes the lawless is a schoolmaster pointing to Christ, in whom alone the sinner is made righteous. Paul as a steward entrusted with the gospel foreshadows every faithful minister who guards the deposit of truth handed down.
basic.christ: The greeting names Christ Jesus our hope, and the whole charge is anchored in the glorious gospel of the blessed God. The law rightly used drives sinners to Christ, and sound teaching is measured by whether it agrees with the good news of what God has done in Him.
basic.god: God is called our Savior already in verse 1, and the gospel is the gospel of the blessed God. He is the source of grace, mercy, and peace, and the owner of the stewardship the gospel advances. He entrusts His truth to servants and calls them to guard it faithfully.
basic.crossReferences: Titus 1 gives the same charge to silence false teachers. Galatians 3 shows the law as a guardian leading us to Christ. Second Timothy 1 speaks of guarding the good deposit entrusted to us.
basic.oneStory: From the start God has spoken truly and been opposed by lies and counterfeits. Here He raises up guardians of the gospel to keep His people anchored to the truth. The law exposes sin, the gospel saves sinners, and the whole letter serves God's long work of building a household of faith around His Son.

context.literary:
The letter has no thanksgiving. Most of Paul's letters move from greeting to a warm paragraph of prayer, but here the greeting runs straight into business, much as it does in Galatians. The urgency is part of the message. Verses 1 and 2 are a single compact salutation, and Paul expands each of the usual parts: his own apostleship rests on a divine command, Timothy is a genuine child, and the familiar blessing gains a third gift, mercy, which Paul adds to grace and peace only in his letters to Timothy.

Verses 3 to 7 are famous for a sentence that never finishes. Paul begins 'As I urged you...' and the main clause that should follow, 'so do it now,' is never spoken. The English 'you should stay on' supplies what the Greek leaves hanging, and Paul swerves to his real subject before he reaches it. The broken grammar sounds like a man writing with a heavy heart.

The paragraph turns on a contrast between a goal and a miss. Verse 5 names the target of all apostolic instruction, and verse 6 describes people who 'have strayed' from it. The aim is spelled out as three things joined together, a pure heart, a clear conscience and a sincere faith, and faith with a good conscience returns in verse 19, so that the passage and the end of the chapter frame each other.

Verses 8 to 11 are again one long sentence, built around the word 'law.' The list of vices in verses 9 and 10 comes in three matched pairs, then moves through specific crimes, then closes with a catch-all, 'anyone else who is averse to sound teaching.' The specific crimes follow the order of the Ten Commandments, from honouring parents through murder, adultery, theft and false witness. The list ends where Paul wants it to, on teaching, and its last word hands over to the gospel in verse 11, which sets up the testimony of verse 12.
context.historical:
Timothy came from Lystra. Acts 16:1 to 3 says his mother was a believing Jewish woman and his father a Greek, and that Paul took him as a travelling companion and circumcised him so that Jews in that region would not stumble. By the time of this letter Timothy has served with Paul for years and has been left in charge at Ephesus while Paul goes on to Macedonia, verse 3. He is young enough that Paul later has to say 'Let no one despise your youth,' 1 Timothy 4:12, so the opening is partly an act of backing: it reminds the church that Timothy stands where Paul put him.

Ephesus was the greatest city of Roman Asia and the home of the great temple of Artemis. Paul had spent about three years there, Acts 19, and when he said farewell to its elders he gave a prophecy that this letter now shows coming true: 'savage wolves will come in among you,' and 'even from your own number, men will rise up and distort the truth,' Acts 20:29 and 30. The troublemakers of 1 Timothy 1 are insiders who want to be 'teachers of the law.' The word is the same one Luke uses of the respected Gamaliel, Acts 5:34, so these men wanted the standing of expert interpreters.

The myths and genealogies suggest a taste for speculative expansion of Israel's Scriptures. Jewish writing of the period retold the patriarchal stories with elaborate family lines, and Titus 1:14 speaks of 'Jewish myths' in the same breath as commands of men.

The vice list would have been familiar. Greek and Roman moralists also drew up catalogues of vices. Paul's list is distinctive because it is organised by the Decalogue. The slave traders of verse 10 were kidnappers, the very crime Exodus 21:16 punishes with death, which mattered in an empire whose economy rested on slavery.
context.canonical:
Paul calls God 'our Savior' in the first line, and that title is an Old Testament claim taken up for the gospel. 'I, yes I, am the LORD, and there is no Savior but Me,' Isaiah 43:11. Mary sings 'God my Savior,' Luke 1:47, and Titus 1:3 and 4 begin with the same pairing this letter uses, God our Savior and Christ Jesus. 1 Timothy 1 is the first of the three Pastoral Letters, and the others take up its themes: the deposit to be guarded in 2 Timothy 1:13 and 14, and the opponents with their myths in Titus 1:10 to 14, and Titus 3:9.

On the law, the passage stands in a long Pauline conversation. The law is 'holy, and the commandment is holy, righteous, and good,' Romans 7:12, yet 'the law merely brings awareness of sin,' Romans 3:20, and 'became our guardian to lead us to Christ,' Galatians 3:24. Love is the fulfilment of it, Romans 13:10 and Galatians 5:14, and Jesus gave the root of that teaching when he said that all the Law and the Prophets hang on loving God and neighbour, Matthew 22:37 to 40.

The 'entrusted' gospel language runs through 1 Corinthians 9:17, Galatians 2:7 and 1 Thessalonians 2:4. The warning about speculation echoes forward in the same letter, 1 Timothy 4:1 to 3 and 6:3 to 5 and 6:20, and in 2 Timothy 4:3 and 4, where people gather teachers 'to suit their own desires' and 'turn aside to myths.'

The story of Ephesus does not end here. Revelation 2:2 to 4 praises the church there for testing false apostles, and then says 'You have abandoned your first love.' Guarding doctrine and keeping love turned out to be one task, and the Ephesians managed the first better than the second.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul wrote to hold a young leader steady and to correct how a whole church measured its teachers. The test he insists on is not cleverness, novelty or technical command of the Scriptures. It is fruit, and the fruit he names is love flowing from a clean conscience and honest faith. A teaching that leaves people proud, quarrelsome and curious has missed the target no matter how learned it sounds.

He also meant Timothy to hear his own authority confirmed. The letter opens by saying that Paul is an apostle 'by the command of God our Savior,' not by his own ambition, and that Timothy is a true child in the faith. Timothy can silence the false teachers because he acts under a commission that came from God through Paul, not because he is personally forceful.

Third, Paul wanted to correct a misuse of the law without throwing the law away. Verse 8 begins with agreement, 'the law is good,' so the church is not to swing from legalism to contempt for Moses. The law has a job, to address the lawless and expose what is wrong, and when it is used for that job it harmonises with the gospel instead of competing with it. Anyone who has watched a church argue over obscure matters while neglecting its neighbours will recognise the problem Paul is addressing.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Some of this passage is a specific assignment and some is a standing principle. The instruction to 'stay on at Ephesus' belongs to Timothy in one city at one time; no one reads it as a command that every pastor must remain where he is. The particular errors, myths and genealogies, describe what troubled Ephesus, and we should be slow to label any modern theory with those names unless it does the same work of feeding speculation at the expense of faith and love.

What carries across is the method of testing. Ask what a teaching produces. Does it lead toward the love, clear conscience and sincere faith of verse 5, or toward the endless arguing of verse 4? That question is prescriptive for any church that wants to stay healthy.

The vice list is descriptive of the people the law was written to confront. It is not a catalogue handed over to be recited against outsiders, and verse 15 in the same chapter makes plain that the one writing the list counts himself among the worst of sinners. It also does not suggest that a believer may ignore the law's moral content: the order of the list follows the Ten Commandments precisely because those commandments still describe what sin is.

debates.question: What were the myths and endless genealogies?

views.label: Jewish legends and legal speculation
views.case: The teachers wanted to be teachers of the law, verse 7, and Titus 1:14 links the myths to 'Jewish myths.' Many read them as imaginative expansions of the Old Testament narratives, with family trees used to build elaborate stories about ancestors. The charge of 'controversies' in 1 Timothy 6:4 and Titus 3:9, where genealogies and quarrels about the law appear together, fits the same milieu.

views.label: Early gnostic style speculation
views.case: Later in the letter Paul warns against 'so-called knowledge,' 6:20, and against forbidding marriage and certain foods, 4:3. Some see in this a blend of Jewish material with speculation about hidden knowledge and the layers of the spiritual world. They note that full gnostic systems belong to the second century, so most call it a forerunner rather than the finished thing.

views.label: A mix that the text does not let us untangle
views.case: Paul never lists the content of the myths, and that silence is itself informative. He objects to the function, not the details: speculation, empty talk and argument. A careful reader can admit that the exact system is unknown without losing the point.

debates.bearing: The pastoral remedy does not wait for a precise identification. Whatever the myths were, they bred speculation instead of stewardship by faith, so the test of verse 5 applies to any teaching that does the same.

debates.question: What is the lawful use of the law in verses 8 to 11?

views.label: The law restrains and exposes sin
views.case: Verse 9 says the law is not enacted for the righteous but for the lawless. On this reading the law's proper work is to confront wrongdoing, put a check on the worst behaviour and show sinners their need, which matches Romans 3:20 and Galatians 3:24. This is how many Reformers described the law's first use, and it gives the vice list its natural place.

views.label: A rebuke of the false teachers' misuse
views.case: The point stresses that the would-be teachers handle the law wrongly. Used lawfully it agrees with the gospel; used as a source of speculation and pride it does not. On this view Paul is guarding the law from its abusers more than he is defining its function.

views.label: The law as the pattern a righteous person already keeps
views.case: Others read 'not enacted for the righteous' as saying that a person led by the Spirit does not need the law as an external threat, because the Spirit produces what the law requires, Galatians 5:22 and 23, Romans 8:4. The law then describes goodness rather than merely policing evil.

debates.bearing: These readings overlap more than they conflict. Each insists that the law is good, that its moral content remains, and that it finds its place under the gospel of Christ rather than over it.

debates.question: How should the word translated 'homosexuals' in verse 10 be understood?

views.label: Same sex intercourse in general
views.case: The Greek word is a compound of 'male' and 'bed,' and the same two words appear side by side in the Greek version of Leviticus 20:13, 'a man lies with a man.' Many conclude that Paul coins a term to refer to the Levitical prohibition, so that it covers male same sex intercourse as such. This is the traditional view and underlies the BSB rendering.

views.label: Exploitative or commercial forms
views.case: Some scholars argue that the word is rare enough that its sense should be settled by context, and propose that it points to men who use others sexually, such as in prostitution or the abuse of boys and slaves. They notice that it stands beside 'slave traders,' which suggests exploitation.

views.label: Uncertain, but plainly a sin the law restrains
views.case: A third group says the evidence for narrowing or widening the term is thin and holds only that the word names a form of sexual sin that the law restrains, like the others in the list.

debates.bearing: Whichever view is taken, the list is there to show what the law addresses, and the next verses say that the gospel reaches 'the worst of sinners,' 1:15. The proper response is neither contempt for those the list names nor silence about what the law says.

study.originalLanguages:
Paul uses the same Greek root for 'instruct' in verse 3 and 'instruction' in verse 5, parangello and parangelia. The first is the verb of a command given with authority, as a commander gives orders. Timothy is to command certain men to stop; but the apostolic command as a whole has a goal, and that goal is love. The shared root means the command to stop false teaching and the goal of love belong together. Discipline here is not an end in itself.

The word 'goal' in verse 5 is telos, the end toward which something is aimed. The word translated 'strayed' in verse 6 is astocheo, built from the negative prefix and the root that means a mark or target. The picture is archery. Love is the target, and those who 'have strayed' have missed it. The verb occurs again in 6:21 and 2 Timothy 2:18, always of people who have missed the truth, which shows that this is a family of words Paul uses for doctrinal drift.

The 'sincere faith' of verse 5 is the adjective anypokritos, 'unhypocritical,' literally a faith with no actor's mask. Paul uses the same word for love in Romans 12:9 and for Timothy's own faith in 2 Timothy 1:5, 'your sincere faith, which first dwelt in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice.' The same word appears in 1 Peter 1:22, 'a genuine love for your brothers.' So the three companions of verse 5 are not external behaviour; they are inward integrity.

In verse 2 Timothy is 'my true child.' The adjective is gnesios, meaning legitimate or genuine, as opposed to a counterfeit or an adopted claim. Paul says the same of Titus, Titus 1:4, and of Timothy in 1 Corinthians 4:17, 'my beloved and faithful child.' The word gives the relationship its force: Timothy is a true heir to what Paul teaches.

In verse 8 the law is good 'if one uses it legitimately.' Greek has a pun here that English cannot catch: the word for 'law,' nomos, is paired with nomimos, 'lawfully,' so the verse says one must use the law lawfully. The adverb occurs again in 2 Timothy 2:5, where an athlete is not crowned unless he competes 'according to the rules.' To use the law lawfully is to use it as it was meant to be used.

Finally, verse 6's 'empty talk' is mataiologia, from mataios, futile, and logos, word: speech with no result, the opposite of a word that bears fruit.

typology.type: The law as guardian toward Christ, 1 Timothy 1:8-11
typology.fulfillment: The law addresses the lawless and exposes their sin, and Paul elsewhere calls it a guardian whose job was to 'lead us to Christ, that we might be justified by faith,' Galatians 3:24. In Israel the law kept the nation in custody and pointed forward. The escalation comes in Christ, who is 'the end of the law, to bring righteousness to everyone who believes,' Romans 10:4, and who came not to abolish the Law but to fulfill it, Matthew 5:17. The pattern falls short at one point: the guardian can show sin but cannot remove it, which only the gospel of verse 11 does.

typology.type: The Ten Commandments behind the vice list, verses 9 and 10
typology.fulfillment: The list of sins follows the order of the Decalogue, from parents through murder, sexual sin, theft and false witness, Exodus 20:12 to 16. Written on stone, the commandments described what God required and could not give the power to keep it. Jeremiah promised a covenant in which God would 'put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts,' Jeremiah 31:33, and Paul says the Corinthians are Christ's letter written 'not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts,' 2 Corinthians 3:3. In Christ the righteous standard of the law is 'fulfilled in us,' Romans 8:4. The type is incomplete without the Spirit.

typology.type: The glory of the gospel and the glory on Moses' face, verse 11
typology.fulfillment: Paul calls the message 'the glorious gospel.' The ministry of the law came with a glory so bright that Israel could not gaze at Moses' face, yet it was 'fleeting glory,' 2 Corinthians 3:7. The gospel is called 'the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God,' 2 Corinthians 4:4, and the glory it carries lasts. The correspondence is that both covenants came with God's glory; the escalation is that the second belongs to a ministry 'even more glorious,' 2 Corinthians 3:8 and 9. The type falls short because Moses' glory faded and he veiled it.

typology.type: Timothy guarding the flock from wolves, verse 3
typology.fulfillment: Paul told the Ephesian elders that 'savage wolves' would come among them, Acts 20:29, and Timothy is now asked to stop the damage. The pattern of a shepherd protecting sheep goes back to David, who defended his father's flock from a lion and a bear, 1 Samuel 17:34 and 35. The fullest version is Jesus, who says that the good shepherd 'lays down His life for the sheep,' while the hired hand runs when the wolf comes, John 10:11 and 12. Timothy is not a second saviour; he is a servant of the one Shepherd, and his guarding is only a reflection of that Shepherd's care.

study.christ:
The letter begins with Christ in its first breath, and Paul describes him by a phrase that is easy to read past: 'Christ Jesus our hope,' verse 1. Colossians 1:27 supplies the explanation, 'Christ in you, the hope of glory.' Hope here is not an attitude but a person. Everything the false teachers are chasing, whether knowledge, status or secret understanding, is found in him alone, which is why their speculations are not harmless extras but a substitute.

Paul joins Christ to God in the same verse. The command that made him an apostle came from 'God our Savior and of Christ Jesus our hope.' One preposition carries both names, so the sentence puts the Father and the Son side by side as joint sources of the apostle's authority. Verse 2 does it again: grace, mercy and peace come 'from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.' The word 'Savior' belongs to the God of Isaiah 43:11, and Titus 2:13 moves in the same direction when it speaks of 'our great God and Savior Jesus Christ.' Paul does not need to argue the point; he assumes it.

The law passage leads to Christ by showing what the law cannot do. It addresses sinners, exposes them and restrains them, and that is its lawful use. It cannot give life, which is why verse 11 turns at once to the gospel. Christ is the one in whom the law's demand is met: 'For Christ is the end of the law, to bring righteousness to everyone who believes,' Romans 10:4. He also lives out the double commandment that gives verse 5 its meaning. When Jesus said that all the Law and the Prophets hang on loving God and loving one's neighbour, Matthew 22:37 to 40, he named the same love that Paul calls the goal of instruction. The apostle's 'goal' is simply the life of Christ reproduced in his people.

The 'glorious gospel' is Christ's own glory made known. 2 Corinthians 4:4 names it 'the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God.' To say that sound teaching agrees with it is to say that sound teaching conforms to the person and work of Christ.

A caution keeps the reading honest. The vice list is not a hidden prophecy of Christ, and the genealogies are not a code. The link is made by the passage's own claims, that the gospel is the measure of every teaching and that Christ is the hope that makes teaching worthwhile.
study.god:
The God of this passage is first of all a God who commands and entrusts. The opening names him as the source of Paul's apostolic commission, and verse 11 closes by saying the gospel was 'entrusted' to Paul. God does not hold his truth in reserve for experts; he gives it to servants to guard and pass on. Responsibility for the message, in other words, is a gift from him.

He is called 'blessed' in verse 11, 'the glorious gospel of the blessed God.' The word means happy in himself, complete and lacking nothing. Paul uses it again at 6:15, 'the blessed and only Sovereign One.' That fullness matters for the argument. A God who lacks nothing does not need human speculation to complete his revelation, and he does not offer his truth in pieces to be assembled by cleverness. The gospel is the overflow of a happy God, not the product of a puzzle.

He is also Savior, and the title opens the letter. Paul does not start with demands. He starts with the God who rescues, and every later instruction rests on that rescue. It is worth noticing that the very commandments Timothy must enforce are given to build up a church that has first been saved.

The passage shows God's concern for truth and for love at the same moment, and refuses to let one swallow the other. The goal is love, but love from a 'clear conscience' and 'sincere faith,' so the God who gives the command cares about sincerity inside as well as conduct outside. He is the one who looks at the heart, as 1 Thessalonians 2:4 puts it, 'God, who examines our hearts.'

The law's presence in the passage says something about his character. Law is 'good' because it expresses his righteousness, Romans 7:12, and it is aimed at murder, theft and lies because he is a God who protects life, property and truth. Its place is not in competition with grace: both come from the same moral Lord, and the same God who exposes sin also pardons it.

For worship, the passage invites us to praise before we do anything else. The next verses burst into thanks, and the shape is a good pattern for a church. We hear God's commission, we examine our teaching by love, and we answer the God who is blessed with our own thanks and dependence.

crossReferences.note: Paul's farewell to the Ephesian elders predicts that 'savage wolves' would come and that men would rise 'from your own number' to distort the truth. 1 Timothy 1:3 to 7 shows the prophecy fulfilled, which explains why Paul takes the problem so seriously and why Timothy is left behind.

A close parallel charge to another young leader, on another island. Titus is to silence men who teach for gain and 'pay no attention to Jewish myths.' The match with 1 Timothy 1:4 suggests a common pattern of error across the Pauline churches.

Paul's own summary of the law: it is 'holy, and the commandment is holy, righteous, and good.' It explains how 1 Timothy 1:8 can say 'the law is good' without contradicting his teaching that no one is justified by it.

The law as a guardian until Christ came. This is the classic text on the lawful use of the law, showing that its function is to hold sinners until faith arrives and to lead them to Christ, which fits the movement from verse 9 to verse 11.

The commandments on parents, murder, adultery, theft and false witness. The vice list of 1 Timothy 1:9 and 10 follows their order, so the apostle is quietly showing that the Decalogue is what the law is really about.

Without love, even prophecy, all knowledge and mountain moving faith leave a person 'nothing.' It supports the claim of verse 5 that the goal of instruction is love, and it explains why the false teachers' learning counted for nothing.
Timothy is told to hold the 'pattern of sound teaching' and to guard the good deposit. It extends the idea of verse 11, the gospel entrusted to Paul, into Timothy's own responsibility to pass it on.

The same test returns at the end of the letter: anyone who teaches another doctrine and rejects sound words is conceited and has an unhealthy interest in controversies. Together the two passages frame the whole letter around true and false teaching.

Jesus praises Ephesus for exposing false apostles, then warns that the church has abandoned its first love. The reader sees that 1 Timothy 1:5, with love as the goal, was necessary for the church that guarded doctrine well.
Jesus teaches that all the Law and the Prophets hang on loving God and loving neighbour. It is the foundation for Paul's claim that love is the goal and that the law finds its meaning in love.

study.oneStory:
The story of Scripture has always involved a word from God and a rival word. In Eden the serpent began with a question about what God had said, and every generation since has faced teachers who reshape the word to fit their own desires. 1 Timothy 1 shows the same contest at a later point in the story. God has spoken in his Son and entrusted that word to apostles; now the question is who will keep it and how.

The passage answers a long standing question about the law. Israel received it at Sinai as a gift, and then watched it become a source of pride for some and despair for others. Paul places it in its proper position in the plot. It is good and holy, it names sin for what it is, and it holds the guilty in view until the promised one comes. It was never a way to earn life, which is why it fits with the gospel of verse 11 and not against it.

The passage also moves the story toward the church as a household. The word translated 'stewardship' in verse 4 is a household word, and the letter will go on to call the church 'God's household,' 3:15. Under the old covenant a nation held the oracles of God; under the new, a people drawn from every nation is entrusted with the gospel, and Timothy's task is the pastoral care of that household. This is the beginning of the chain that leads to 2 Timothy 2:2, where the teaching is passed to faithful men who will teach others.

The same passage looks ahead to the end of the story. The aim of all instruction, love from a pure heart, is what the new creation will be full of. Paul's picture of a people marked by a pure heart, a clear conscience and a sincere faith is a small preview of the day when sin and deceit are gone. Until then, Scripture's last word about Ephesus, Revelation 2:4, warns that even a church sound in doctrine can lose its love, and so the church must keep the target in sight and keep praying for the one who enables it, the Savior who has promised to bring his people home.

quiz.q: Why did Paul leave Timothy at Ephesus?

options.text: To instruct certain men not to teach a different doctrine.
options.note: This is Paul's stated charge in verses 3 and 4.

options.text: To raise money for the Jerusalem church.
options.note: A real Pauline concern elsewhere, but not the reason given here; the issue is false teaching.

options.text: To plant a brand new church in the city.
options.note: The Ephesian church already existed; Timothy was to guard and order it.

options.text: To wait quietly until Paul returned.
options.note: He was left for active, demanding work of correction, not idle waiting.

quiz.q: What is the goal of true instruction, according to Paul?

options.text: Love that comes from a pure heart, a clear conscience, and a sincere faith.
options.note: Verse 5 names love as the aim, springing from these three.

options.text: Winning every argument with the false teachers.
options.note: Error must be corrected, but the aim is love, not victory in debate.

options.text: Mastering myths and genealogies more thoroughly than others.
options.note: These are exactly what Paul warns against as mere speculation.

options.text: Keeping the deepest teaching hidden from ordinary believers.
options.note: Nothing here hides truth; the goal is love built on sincere faith.

quiz.q: What does Paul say about the law?

options.text: The law is good, if one uses it lawfully, to expose the lawless.
options.note: Verses 8 and 9 affirm the law is good when used as intended.

options.text: The law is bad and should be discarded by Christians.
options.note: Paul says the opposite; the fault is misuse, not the law itself.

options.text: The law saves the righteous who keep it well.
options.note: The law exposes sin; it is not a ladder of self-righteousness.

options.text: The law has nothing to do with the gospel.
options.note: Sound teaching, and the lawful use of the law, agree with the gospel.

quiz.q: What test does Paul give for sound teaching?

options.text: It agrees with the glorious gospel of the blessed God.
options.note: Verse 11 makes the gospel the measure of sound doctrine.

options.text: It sounds impressive and confident.
options.note: The false teachers were confident, verse 7, yet did not understand what they said.

options.text: It is popular with the crowd.
options.note: Popularity is no gauge of truth; agreement with the gospel is.

options.text: It offers new speculation beyond Scripture.
options.note: Speculation is the error; sound teaching agrees with the gospel.

quiz.q: What went wrong with those who strayed from the goal of instruction?

options.text: They turned aside to empty talk, wanting to teach what they did not understand.
options.note: Verses 6 and 7 describe empty talk and confident ignorance.

options.text: They simply preferred a quieter style of worship.
options.note: The problem was false doctrine and empty talk, not style.

options.text: They cared too much about love and not enough about rules.
options.note: The reverse; they missed love, the goal, and chased speculation.

options.text: They taught the plain gospel too boldly.
options.note: They departed from sound teaching; the gospel was not their problem.

questions: Paul says the goal of all instruction is love from a pure heart. When you learn or teach the Bible, is love the aim, or can knowledge become an end in itself?
The false teachers were confident but did not understand what they were saying. Where might confidence be outrunning real understanding in your own speech about God?
A clear conscience is named as one spring of genuine love. Is there anything troubling your conscience that you need to bring honestly to God?
The law is good when used lawfully, to expose sin and drive us to Christ. How has seeing your own sin more clearly deepened your gratitude for the gospel?
Paul was entrusted with the gospel as a stewardship. What has God entrusted to you that you are responsible to guard and pass on faithfully?

translationNotes.note: The BSB footnote gives the literal phrase rather than the stewardship of God in faith, underlining that oikonomia means God's ordered saving plan received by faith.
For slave traders carries a footnote reading or for kidnappers; the term denotes those who seize and sell human beings.
Sound teaching translates a word meaning healthy or wholesome, a recurring image in the Pastoral Epistles for doctrine that gives spiritual health.
